About this citation

Only the seven 'inner chapters' are generally accepted as Zhuangzi's own; the outer and miscellaneous chapters are the work of a school. Which layer a passage comes from is part of what the locator tells a reader.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Zhuangzi, Discussion on Making All Things Equal and files it under Daoism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Zhuangzi

Zhuangzi (Zhuang Zhou, c. 369–c.

Interpretation

This belongs to Zhuangzi's "equalising" discussion, where he argues that the distinctions people treat as fixed — this versus that, right versus wrong — depend on the standpoint from which they are drawn. His claim is not that all views are equally true but that each is conditioned by a perspective, so treating one's own as final is a mistake about what kind of thing a judgement is. The equality is of status as perspectives, not of merit.

Why it matters

It is a remedy for a specific failure: the confidence that comes from never having seen the question from the other side.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Heaven and earth were born together with me,…”?

“Heaven and earth were born together with me,…” comes from Zhuangzi, Discussion on Making All Things Equal (Qiwulun 齊物論) (c. 4th–3rd century BCE; outer and miscellaneous chapters later), attributed to Zhuangzi.

What does Zhuangzi mean by equality?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Mary Wollstonecraft and John Locke), equality is framed through Feminist Philosophy and British Empiricism. Some passages define equality; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through equality, freedom.
